claims.text: Eutectic high-entropy alloys have dual-phase lamellar colonies containing numerous internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
Undoped eutectic high-entropy alloys with conventional dual-phase lamellar colonies exhibit brittle behavior at room temperature.
Adding 0.1–0.3 atomic % boron during melting will cause boron to segregate selectively to internal lamellar boundaries.
Homogenization at 1100°C for 1 hour followed by rapid quenching will preserve the boron-segregated interfacial state.
Boron segregation lowers the energy of internal lamellar boundaries.
Boron segregation reinforces interfacial cohesion at internal lamellar boundaries.
Improved interfacial cohesion reduces microcrack nucleation at lamellar interfaces.
Improved interfacial bonding produces more uniform stress transfer between lamellae.
Reduced microcrack nucleation and more uniform stress transfer mitigate premature tensile failure.
The proposed boron treatment enables improved plastic deformation.
Boron-doped material will have greater room-temperature tensile strength than the undoped baseline.
Boron-doped material will have greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the undoped baseline.
Boron-doped material will develop fewer and smaller interfacial microcracks during tensile loading than the undoped baseline.
The beneficial effects occur only within a narrow boron concentration window of 0.1–0.3 atomic %.
High-temperature homogenization and rapid quenching are critical for obtaining the predicted benefit.
Departures from the proposed boron range or processing route may eliminate the benefit or cause embrittlement.
